opus-5.5.text:
Well, I can't speak for OpenAI, and I don't know their internal reasoning. But I can share how I'd think about a decision like that from the outside.

Every company has finite resources: compute, people, and leadership attention. Right now coding is one of the clearest places where these models create obvious, measurable value. Developers pay for it, the feedback loop is tight, and you can tell quickly whether the model got better. Coding is also closely tied to the broader agenda of building agents that do real work. So if you're a company that needs revenue and a clear path forward, concentrating there makes a lot of sense.

Video generation is different. It's extremely compute-hungry to train and to serve. And the business model is still being figured out. There's a lot of excitement, and the demos are spectacular, but turning that into a sustainable product is hard. A consumer app built around generated videos is a very different business from a developer tool.

That said, I'd separate "video generation as a product" from "video models as world models." I think they're related but not the same. From my perspective, the deeper value of learning to generate video is that the model has to learn how the world works: physics, object permanence, cause and effect, how agents move and interact. That's essential for physical AI, for robots and autonomous vehicles, where you need to simulate, predict, and generate training data. That direction isn't going away. If anything, it's getting more important.

So I wouldn't read it as "video doesn't matter." I'd read it as a company with a particular mission and business making a prioritization call. Different organizations will place different bets. For people working on embodied intelligence, world models are core infrastructure, not a side product. The field is big enough that it doesn't depend on any single company's choice.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I'd say I don't have inside knowledge of how that decision was made, so I can only read it from the outside. But I don't think it's that surprising, and I don't think it says video generation doesn't matter.

Every lab has finite compute, finite researchers, and finite attention. If you look at where the revenue is today, it's coding. Developers pay for it, enterprises pay for it, and the feedback loop is very clean. You can verify whether code works. That makes it an ideal target for reinforcement learning, and it compounds. The better your model is at coding, the faster your own team moves. So for a company that has to fund frontier training runs, concentrating there is a rational business decision.

Video is different. It is enormously expensive. The tokens are much heavier than text, the inference cost is high, and the consumer market for generated clips is still finding its footing. People are impressed for a week, and then the question becomes, what do I actually do with this every day? Sora was a wonderful demonstration of scaling diffusion transformers, and I think the whole field learned from it. But as a product, the path to monetization was less obvious than coding.

Where I would push back is on the idea that this is a retreat from video as a research direction. I come at it from a different angle. For us at NVIDIA, video generation was never primarily about entertainment. It's about building world models, systems that understand physics, how objects move, how scenes change when you act in them. That's the foundation for robotics and autonomous vehicles. Those are areas where you cannot collect enough real data, so you have to simulate, and a generative model that understands the physical world becomes a data engine and a planner at the same time.

So I actually see OpenAI's move as a kind of specialization in the industry. Some labs will go deep on language and agents. Others will go deep on the physical world. Both are needed. And honestly, the modeling techniques transfer. The architectures, the tokenizers, the post-training methods, they cross over. A breakthrough in one area tends to help the other within a year or two.

If anything, I'd say the lesson is about focus. The era where one lab tries to do everything at the frontier is probably ending, because the cost of each frontier is now so high. You have to decide what you want to be the best in the world at. OpenAI made their choice. We've made ours.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the resource decision from the broader research question. If OpenAI is pulling back from Sora to focus on coding, I would read that primarily as a decision about where it sees the clearest near-term return—not as proof that video generation is a dead end.

Coding has a relatively direct feedback loop. You generate code, run it, test it, and see whether it solves the problem. There’s also a clear customer need: if a tool helps people build software faster or maintain it more effectively, that value is easier to measure and charge for.

Video generation is valuable too, but generating an impressive clip and becoming an indispensable part of a production workflow are different milestones. You need control, consistency, and the ability to make precise changes. Those are challenging problems, and pursuing them takes resources.

So the strategic logic could be quite straightforward: concentrate on a product with clearer demand and measurable utility. But I’d be cautious about inferring their internal reasoning without more information. And I wouldn’t equate that product choice with a judgment that learning from video is unimportant. Understanding motion, physical interactions, and how the world changes over time remains a substantial research problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I would separate two questions: whether that is the right decision for OpenAI as a company, and what it tells us about video generation as a technology. Those are different questions.

If OpenAI is pulling back from Sora to focus on coding, I would read that primarily as a resource allocation decision. Coding has a relatively clear feedback loop: you generate code, run it, test it, and see whether it solves the problem. There is also a direct connection between a better model and something a customer is willing to pay for.

Video is harder to evaluate. A clip can look beautiful, but making it follow a precise creative intention, remain consistent, and fit into a production workflow is a different challenge. The impressive demo and the useful product are not necessarily the same thing.

But I would be careful about concluding that video generation is therefore less important. Understanding motion, physical interactions, and how a scene changes over time could be valuable well beyond making videos. The question is how much of that understanding a model actually learns, and how we can measure it.

So, strategically, concentrating resources can make sense. You cannot pursue every direction with equal intensity. But a company's decision about where to invest is not a final verdict on which research direction will matter most.
